description_full: Shoe Station Group Inc., together with its subsidiaries, retails footwear in the United States. Its products include shoes, sneakers, heels, sandals, boots, work and safety shoes, and athletic shoes; and accessories for men, women and kids. It sells its products through stores, online, and mobile app. The company was formerly known as Shoe Carnival, Inc. and changed its name to Shoe Station Group Inc. in June 2026. Shoe Station Group Inc. was founded in 1978 and is headquartered in Fort Mill, South Carolina.

financial_summary: Shoe Station Group, Inc. is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $390M market cap on $1.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -3% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 15% against a 10% cost of capital, a 6-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 30%.

The business throws off $27M in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.36× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 34% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (7%).

mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 22% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 34% below the high.

growth: Revenue has compounded at -3.5% over 3 years, 1.8% over 5 years and 1.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.

Free cash flow has compounded -11.3% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.3x, 3.9% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 4, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.

own: Insiders own 33.5%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 78%.

It returns 4.2% a year to shareholders (4.7% in dividends).

It has paid a dividend for 13 consecutive years, raising it 24.2% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 53.1% of the float, 10.8 days to cover.
people: With about 2,300 employees, each generates about $494K of revenue, 1.3x the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 2.9% a year across its filed history.

CEO pay is $188K (0x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
